On schedule C:

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?']

Under schedule C we have an item for legislation in the House of Commons. The item gives me an opportunity to make some remarks upon the suggestions that were raised in the House of Commons the other day by the Prime Minister in relation to prospective changes in what might be called the make-up of the chamber. I just wanted at this time to express some of the difficulties I think these changes will create. For one thing, if we turn the chamber into one like the British have with benches, there will need to be a great reduction in the size of this chamber; that is if we are going to keep it in relation to the British example. I should like all members of all parties, before they become too enthusiastic about this idea of the Prime Minister, to think about the relative discomfort of the benches. Any of you who have been in Westminster and have observed the activities in the British House of Commons will recognize that their attendance in the House of Commons is no better than ours, if as good; that it is only on major debates that you get a crowd; that ordinarily there is a mere handful in the house. Despite all the reverence that many people feel toward the mother of parliaments, I would suggest that in many ways they do a rather different kind of work than is done by the members of the House of Commons in this particular country.
Furthermore, one of the marked differences between the British House of Commons and the Canadian House of Commons stems from their whole parliamentary set-up. The next step which the Prime Minister may be suggesting is to cut us out from any offices because in Britain they do not happen to have offices. About the only thing a British member of parliament has is a little locker to hang his hat in. If he wants to interview any constituents, he does so out in the corridors, in the lobbies or in the public rooms. You can let this love for British tradition and British set-up take us a little too far. I should not like to suggest by these criticisms of the British system as they relate to Canada that I think their system is wrong. I think it is fine for them. It suits their particular kind of country which has a unitary form of government that is highly centralized, and in which the centre of the government is so close to the people in terms of distance and time. But I would suggest that in our country our terms are very much different.
Ways and Means
But on the main point of the Prime Minister with regard to introducing benches, I should like to point out again that benches are very uncomfortable and they lead to the display, as any of you who have watched proceedings in the British House of Commons will know, of a great deal of masculine leg. I would suggest it is much more undignified than what we Canadians are used to. I feel that we are very strong on dignity and decorum. If any of you have ever seen the exposed lower legs of Winston Churchill or some of the other gentlemen, you would recognize that it is not an aesthetic display at all. I do not feel that we need to go that far in order to do what the Prime Minister wants to achieve, that is to shorten the debates in this House of Commons. It was delightful of the Prime Minister, to suggest that the debates needed shortening, to admit that he was himself guilty of being prolix at times, but I do feel that before this idea gets very far at all, every one of us from a non-partisan point of view should go over it very carefully.
I would make this suggestion. It might apply to many of you and certainly would apply to myself. I would be uncomfortable in speaking if I did not know that I had something to lean on, something to prop myself up against. If I were exposed in a much smaller amphitheatre, more like a bull ring and closer to the swirl of battle, it might often mean that we would be closer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in a much reduced ring, and that with our rather different temperaments and different ideas of sportsmanship and gamesmanship from those which the British have it might lead to fisticuffs or something like that if we went too far in altering the chamber. So I just wanted to make the point that I think this is one change or suggested change or trial balloon in connection with the House of Commons that every member wants to be very careful about considering.
There is one other point that I wanted to make under schedule C. It has to do with mines and technical surveys, surveys and mapping branch. We were given assurance by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) last year, when his estimates were before the house, that every effort was made to see that there was not any overlapping between the provincial efforts in the geological mapping field and the federal efforts. Yet is was just several weeks ago that Mr. Rickaby, who is an official of the Ontario provincial government devoted to work in this field, came out with the statement that the crying need in this particular field was federal leadership to wipe

Ways and Means
out what he called overlapping and a complete failure to get a plan. Mr. Rickaby made the same point as did Mr. Brown who works for Spartan Air Services before the Senate land use committee, that we have no plans at all for mapping our geological resources, not in a way that compares with what the Russians have already done. Both those gentlemen talked in terms of two and three decades behind the Russians. In the light of the minister's statement last year that there was not any overlapping and that there was consultation, I feel that this is one problem in connection with this particular department in connection with which we need a new approach and at which we need a new look.
One of the difficulties in connection with a geological survey, a land use survey or a forest aerial survey is that there is a great deal of overlapping. One of the most interesting developments in connection with the work is that now photographic interpretation experts can look at aerial photographs and not only draw conclusions about the stands of forests that may be there but from the stands of forests and the vegetation picture they can come to very definite conclusions about the type of soil and the whole environment. Because of this interrelationship of the geological aspect, the mineral aspect, the soil aspect and the forest aspect which fit in; and because our Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is supporting by subsidy provincial efforts in this photographic field as far as forestry is concerned; and because each one of the provinces is undertaking geological surveys and aerial mapping and because our federal Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is doing that, it seems to me that we should have what Mr. Rickaby called for, namely a meeting of the minds involved and some attempt to give us a co-ordinated program that would finally lead to the kind of survey giving us the kind of information which we need for land use in Canada and which we do not have at the present time.
It seems to me that this kind of concrete program should have formed one prominent corner of the vision or, as the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) would call it, the mosaic. In any event a corner of the mosaic should, I think, be a co-ordinated program related to mapping and geological survey work. This, in my opinion, would be most worth-while.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution contemplates the introduction of a bill which is of an annual nature. As the house is aware, the Canadian National Railways borrow from the government to meet their financial requirements; they borrow to meet their capital budget requirements and in those years when they have need of financial assistance, to meet their operating budget they also borrow for that purpose from the government.
The capital budget is reviewed and passed on by the government as a matter of course, but all of these budgetary requirements of the Canadian National Railways, indeed all their affairs, are submitted to the house and for many years it has been the practice of the house to appoint a special committee to review the operations and the financial affairs of the Canadian National Railways system. It is an annual accounting to parliament. It is the equivalent in the procedures attaching to corporations that are not of a public nature to the annual shareholders' meeting.
At this session such a committee was appointed and it held meetings, lengthy meetings, on July 14 and 15 last. The president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, and other officials of the Canadian National Railways, Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, and Trans-Canada Air Lines were present with representatives of the auditors of the system. They gave their testimony and answered questions covering the whole broad field of the operations of the associated companies. In

the course of those proceedings the committee also reviewed the budget of the company.
This bill follows, in accordance with the annual practice of the house, that review, that accounting from the company before the special committee. The bill itself, in accordance with the annual practice in such matters, covers the financial requirements of the company for the current calendar year of 1958. The fiscal year of the company is the calendar year, but because of the arrangement with respect to the sittings of parliament it is necessary in these bills also to make provision in advance for the estimated financial needs of the Canadian National system for the first six months of the following calendar year. Accordingly, this bill makes provision not only for the financial requirements for the year 1958 but also for the first six months of the calendar year 1959 of the Canadian National system.
The bill, as is indicated in this resolution, provides for authorizations, guarantees and loans; it also provides, although this is not part of the resolution, for the appointment of the auditors of the company.
As I indicated earlier this afternoon, there is very great urgency attached to this bill, and if it meets with the approval of the house, without asking any hon. member to curtail any of his rights, we hope that this house may be prepared to facilitate the passage of the measure through all stages today. That suggestion was put before the house last night by the leader of the house.
The reason is simply that because of the fact that the session is so much later than usual this year the bill is coming before the house somewhat later than normal according to the calendar, although it is well up in the business of the session in terms of the sessional calendar. It could not have been brought forward, of course, until the committee had completed its review of the needs of the Canadian National system for the funds which this bill will permit the Minister of Finance to loan to the company. It is extremely urgent at the present time-extremely urgent-that this bill be passed through all stages in both houses and receive royal assent not later than the first day of next week unless the company is to be compelled to resort to bank borrowing. This would not be desirable and I think the house will realize the urgency of the situation which I have endeavoured to put before the committee at this time.
The bill simply takes the usual form; it is a bill well established in form and purpose and the procedure followed with respect to the review and the consideration of the provisions of the budget by the special committee established by the house for that purpose is
Canadian National Railways the established procedure. I trust that having regard to the fact that the need is urgent, that the procedure followed is a time honoured procedure, and that the form of the bill is the well established form of a bill that is annual, the committee will see fit to give it speedy passage.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks on this resolution will be brief. I agree with the first part of the minister's remarks, that this resolution precedes an annual bill to refinance the operations of the Canadian National Railways. It is true that following the usual practice after the establishment of the committee on railways and shipping in the House of Commons, that committee does hear evidence about the operations of the railway, and members of that committee are given the opportunity of considering, discussing and examining the witnesses who come before it.
However, I will point out to the committee that this is only one of the opportunities hon. members have of discussing matters concerning the Canadian National Railways. There are many other opportunities, and I am sure that those members on this side of the house who will wish to take advantage of those opportunities will propose not to do so on this occasion, and that is the reason why I find myself in complete disagreement with the minister in so far as the last part of his remarks are concerned.
Before I come to that, there are on this resolution, a number of things which I believe can usefully be discussed; the financial condition of the railway, the position in which it finds itself concerning the volume of traffic, the freight, which is declining to a marked and _ sharp degree, as was told us by the president of the railway during the hearings of the committee, the lay-offs of certain employees in the various shops from one part of the country to the other, pensions-as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River so well points out-an increase in which had been promised by the government when it was in opposition and during two election campaigns and so on. I might add that the Minister of Transport said the other day the government was still giving consideration to this matter, but no action has been taken.
I do not want to delay the passage of this resolution by discussing these matters, but I do want to object strenuously to this resolution and the bill which follows going through all stages at this time. We on this side of the house are going to protest that, and I will tell the hon. gentleman why.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course, that could only be done by unanimous consent. The suggestion was made last night by the

Canadian National Railways leader of the house, but if the non. gentleman is not willing, all we can hope to do today is to have the resolution reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
We are not willing, and I think the Minsiter of Finance should know why we are not willing. We are not willing because if this committee had been established at the time it should have been established it would not have been necessary to ask for the passage of this bill through all its various stages at this time. What I mean is this- and I say it with all respect to the Minister of Transport-I believe that on at least three occasions he told the president of the C.N.R. that a meeting would take place on such and such a date. The meeting never took place, perhaps because of reasons over which the Minister of Transport had no control or, perhaps, for reasons over which the government had no control. But certainly if that meeting had taken place at the proper time when it was first called these matters could have been given consideration and the bill would have gone through long before this day. That is one of the reasons why we on this side cannot consent to the passage of the bill through all its stages today.
Then, again, there is a very important reason, namely that some, nay many, of the activities and operations of the Canadian National Railway are likely to be discussed at the bill stage, so I do not want to present the appearance of trying to hold up the resolution. That is not my purpose. I realize that after the operations of the C.N.R. have been discussed in committee it is right that the annual bill should be passed thereafter, but on the other hand the advantage and the privilege of members of parliament are such that when any of the stages of a bill come before the house it is up to them to determine whether or not they will take part in the discussion. For that reason we on this side do not propose to allow the bill to go through all its stages at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman agreeable that the resolution should pass today so that we can have the bill distributed tonight?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think there will be any objection to that from this side.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In connection with this resolution, one of the reasons we intended to discuss this matter was because of the evidence which was presented by Mr. Gordon before the committee, evidence which raised serious questions especially in connection with labour and, in particular, in relation to a statement that when central traffic control

was established there was the possibility that the running trades would be reduced even further.
I think everyone in the House of Commons is aware of the difficulties which exist at the present time with regard to dispensing with the services of firemen on diesels. With the prospects of central traffic control it seems to me we are rushing very quickly into an extremely difficult labour problem, and we have a responsibility here to discuss this question and face up to it. It is about time the House of Commons gave some leadership rather than that it should again be presented with the spectacle of the Minister of Labour hopping around, I would say in a not too dignified fashion, in an attempt to avert a nationwide strike-efforts which would end up, in their final phase, in the Prime Minister's room. If any hon. members thought that the brotherhood of railway firemen have put up an effective fight and have raised a lot of issues-irrespective of whatever view one happens to take

I can assure hon. members that the brotherhood of railway trainmen is an even stronger and more formidable organization. What Mr. Gordon hinted at in his report spells labour trouble of as intensive a kind as we have had in Canada during the last few decades and for that reason the whole subject merits a great deal of discussion at the next stage of these proceedings.

subsubtopic: NEW BASIS FOR ASSESSMENT OF SUCCESSION DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the minutes of the committee on banking and commerce will indicate, I took rather strong exception to what I thought was a too fast process in proceeding with the discussion of this bill without adequate knowledge among the people in the country who were concerned about the issues involved. I believe that as events developed my contention was not improper because only after we were concluding our deliberations did we receive from the outside public representations on the new bill, Bill No. C-37, that developed from Bill No. 248 which was so commendably presented to the public by the minister at the last session of the House of Commons.
I wish to say to the minister that my views as expressed as a member of the parliamentary committee on banking and commerce are all the more confirmed when I realize that last week if the minister felt that this had priority among his budget legislation he could have put it at the top of the list. He did not do so. He told the committee that this was a matter of urgent necessity. He said it was something that would have to go to the other house where public hearings were likely to take place and his excuse was that there was extreme urgency. I just remind hon. members of this committee that two or three weeks have gone by now and in the interim I have seen nothing that confirms the view of the minister about the urgency of debate on this particular subject in the parliamentary committee.
I protested the committee sitting a day or two after the presentation of the bill; I said that we were hasty. I protested that a great number of serious-thinking people across this land who had given time and thought to the former draft of the bill, Bill No. 248 of the 1958 session, did not know that we were seriously as a House of Commons considering the new draft. I attempted to make the point that while the Minister of Finance had said that he and his officials had looked over this situation very carefully at great length and had pondered it and were satisfied that this

Estate Tax Act
was in the public interest, there were manifest amendments between Bill No. 248 which was presented and the bill we have now and I suggested that this indicated that public attitudes on a matter of this kind were worthy of consideration and should be welcomed.
Despite all those protests we hurried into a discussion in committee stage in the banking and commerce committee of the bill which was referred to the committee by the House of Commons. I still regret that situation. I think that so many suggestions could have been suggested to the minister after first reading was given to Bill No. 248 that he should have had equal respect for the opportunity of the public to look fit and perhaps criticize his revised version which we now have before us. I know that this bill will go before the Senate committee. I just hope that they will not be so stultified in their thinking that they will refrain from listening to the people from outside who might tell us something about it.
The minister knows that those associated with him at the moment are the same people that I took great pride in having had some association with in the recent past. It is instinctive in my thinking that sometimes it is possible that simplification on the part of those drafting a bill means simplification for them and not necessarily for the general public.
This is the first session of a new parliament. Large numbers of the members of the banking and commerce committee had never before attended a meeting such as we were attending. I want to say that it gave me a great deal of delight and a thrill indeed to find that after-but this was too abrupt, too quick-certain presentations were made in this committee the new members of the House of Commons realized that they had a great opportunity on an occasion such as that to amend a bill such as the one we have before us now if, in their opinion, it was not necessarily in the public interest. I admire very sincerely the attitude taken by some of the members of the banking and commerce committee who had never sat on a committee of this kind before. They heard certain representations from reputable bodies which could not be quoted directly but had to be quoted by a member of the committee for the record in criticism of the view of the administration that simplification is of the essence. I admired particularly the attitude of some of the new members of the House of Commons when they recognized that under the new bill we have not got a definite discharge of liability for
an executor. They rallied to the cause; they persuaded the minister that the bill was not perfect.
Mr. Fleming [Eglinfon): I think my hon. friend will be fair enough to say that the minister was quite prepared to accept amendments, and did accept actually seven amendments, and offered some of them himself, by way of improvement of the bill.

Yes, that is perfectly true, Mr. Chairman, but it just confirms my point when I say that this bill was advanced to the committee stage in unseemly haste.
I want to say that the public at large was not aware that this was under discussion. At least even some members of the committee had not the opportunity to have criticisms of the new bill, although they had, of course, criticisms of the bill introduced in January.
